title: Iona
hook: a Scottish community on an old monastic island: worship, justice and work together

segments.voice: Yesterday, Taizé chant: one short line, sung until it sings you. Your line was repetition is rest. Did your line come back to you somewhere in the day? Day one thousand one hundred seventy-eight.

A small island off the west coast of Scotland, wind and sheep and white sand. Tradition says an Irish monk named Columba landed here and built a monastery, and that for a very long time the island was a place of prayer. Much later, the old abbey stood roofless. Then a Glasgow minister named George MacLeod brought a strange crew out to the island: young ministers in training and out-of-work craftsmen. They rebuilt the abbey together, eating together, praying together, carrying stone side by side. Out of that work came a community that still bears the island's name. Today: Iona.

The Iona Community isn't mainly people living on the island. Its members are scattered, living ordinary lives in cities and towns, and what holds them together is a shared rule. They keep daily prayer and Bible reading. They account to one another for how they spend their money and their time. They meet. And they commit to work for justice and peace. That last part stands out. At Iona, prayer and politics aren't kept in separate rooms. The prayers there name wars, prisons, poverty and the earth, by name. The conviction behind it reaches back to the prophets. Amos hears God speak to a people whose festivals were full while the poor were crushed in the courts: "Take thou away from me the noise of thy songs; for I will not hear the melody of thy viols." And then the line that follows: "But let judgment run down as waters, and righteousness as a mighty stream." Judgment there means justice, fair dealing in the courts. The worship was beautiful. The problem was everything outside it. Micah puts it briefly: "what doth the LORD require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?" Christians weigh this differently. Some keep the church well away from politics, wary that faith gets used by one party or another. Others, like the Iona Community, hold that a prayer for peace that never touches how a city is run hasn't finished its sentence. Both want the gospel kept from being bent. They draw the line in different places.

Here's the practice: pray for justice and peace. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one place far away where people are living through war or injustice. Hold it a while, without rushing to fix it. Then bring to mind one place close to home: a street, a school, a courtroom, a shelter. If you pray, you can hold both before God, and use Amos's words: let judgment run down as waters. If you don't, hold both with care, and ask what one small act of fairness you could make this week. The bell holds the time.
Iona. An island off Scotland, and a scattered Christian community that keeps worship and the work of justice together.

Your line: prayer and politics. Today, read one news story slowly, all the way through, and let it turn into a prayer or a promise instead of one more scroll. Day one thousand one hundred seventy-eight.
